topic: EMD exemption: when MSEs and startups don't pay bid security
draft:
Before you arrange an EMD, read one clause twice: the exemption clause.

Under Rule 170 of GFR 2017, bid security (EMD) is ordinarily 2% to 5% of the estimated value, and micro and small enterprises are exempt from it. In November 2020 the Department of Expenditure told central ministries to ask for a Bid Security Declaration instead of bid security, for tenders issued until 31 December 2021. Buyers still differ: some ask for an EMD, some for a declaration, so the tender itself decides what applies to you.

On GeM bids, the exemption comes with conditions. Bid documents we have read say:
1. Only manufacturers of the goods, or providers of the service, qualify under MSE. Traders do not.
2. You must upload the document for your category (Udyam for MSEs, DPIIT recognition for startups) with the bid.
3. State government buyers may still ask MSEs for an EMD if their additional terms say so.

So the check before every bid is three questions: is there an EMD or a declaration, am I in an exempt category for this item, and which page asks for the proof?

TenderTez lists the EMD clause and the exemption conditions from a tender PDF with the page they are on, so you can check them yourself: https://tendertez.in/?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=emd_exemption

Sources: Department of Expenditure OM on bid security (12 Nov 2020); GFR 2017 Rule 170; a GeM bid document (RRI, GeM-Bidding-5263261).
Before the scope of work, read the eligibility section: turnover years, similar-work definition, and the proof each one needs. If you don't qualify, the rest of the tender doesn't matter.

A turnover clause has four parts, and bids fail on each of them:

1. Which financial years: the last three, or three of the last five?
2. Average or every year: an average lets one weak year pass; "each year" does not.
3. Whole company or the tendered item: some tenders ask for turnover of the subject item only.
4. Proof: audited statements, a CA certificate in a set format, or both.

Then check the corrigenda. Turnover thresholds are one of the things corrigenda change.

topic: Bid Security Declaration instead of EMD
draft:
Some tenders ask for a Bid Security Declaration instead of an EMD. Check which one yours asks for.

In November 2020 the Department of Expenditure told central ministries to keep only a Bid Security Declaration in bid documents, for tenders issued until 31 December 2021. Buyers still differ, so the tender decides.

What a declaration means for you: no money is blocked, but if you withdraw or change your bid during its validity, you can be suspended from that buyer's tenders for the period the tender states.

So read two lines in every tender: does it ask for an EMD or a declaration, and what is the suspension period?

Source: Department of Expenditure office memorandum on bid security, 12 Nov 2020.

"Similar work" is defined in the tender, not by you. Read the definition: type of work, minimum value per order, client type (govt/PSU), and the period. Then match each past order to it before you bid.

MSE purchase preference and the MSE EMD exemption are for manufacturers and service providers. Traders, distributors, sole agents and works contracts are outside the MSE procurement policy. Check your role for the item before you claim it.

A turnover clause has four parts, and bids fail on each: which years (last 3, or 3 of the last 5), average or every year, whole company or the tendered item, and the proof asked for. Then check the corrigenda.

Question for tender consultants and bid managers: which part of preparing a bid takes your team the longest? Reading the tender, collecting documents from the client, annexures, or checking corrigenda?

I am building TenderTez for the reading and checking part, and I would rather build what you actually need. Replies or DMs welcome.

Bids get rejected on form, not just on price: an unsigned annexure, a missing self-attested page, an EMD in the wrong format, an expired certificate. Make a checklist from the tender itself before you upload.

If you are a registered MSE, read the purchase preference clause in central tenders.

Under the Public Procurement Policy for MSEs, an MSE that quotes within L1+15% can be allowed to match the L1 price and supply up to 25% of the tender value. The policy also sets an annual target for central ministries and CPSEs to buy from MSEs.

Three things to check in the tender:
1. Does the clause apply to this item (works contracts are outside the policy)?
2. Are you a manufacturer or service provider for it (traders are excluded)?
3. What proof must be uploaded, and on which page is that asked?

Source: Public Procurement Policy for MSEs Order, 2012, and the Ministry of MSME's FAQ on it.

TenderTez lists such clauses with their page: https://tendertez.in/?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=mse_preference

Make in India preference in central procurement: a Class-I local supplier has at least 50% local content, Class-II at least 20%, unless the nodal ministry sets higher. Below that is non-local. Check which classes the tender accepts.
Under GFR 2017 Rule 170, bid security normally stays valid for 45 days beyond the bid validity period. If a buyer extends bid validity, check whether your EMD or bank guarantee needs extending too.

Before you quote, read the BOQ against the specifications, not on its own.

1. Units: a rate per metre, per number or lump sum changes your price completely.
2. Items marked "as per specification": find that clause and read it.
3. Quantities written as "LS" or "1 No.": ask in the pre-bid meeting what is included.
4. Items that appear in the scope of work but not in the BOQ: someone will have to pay for them.

Every tender has at least three dates that matter: the pre-bid meeting (questions), bid submission close, and technical bid opening. Some add a separate date for physical EMD or documents. Put all of them in your calendar.

draft:
A generic tender checklist misses what this tender asks for. Build it from the tender:

2. Every annexure, signed and stamped as the tender says.
3. EMD or declaration, in the form the tender accepts.
4. Certificates with their validity on the closing date.
